etymology: English; Robert from the Germanic Hrodebert, “bright in fame,” and Morrison, “son of Morris.” A Northumberland labourer’s son (1782–1834) whom the LORD sent as the first Protestant missionary to China.
biblical_def: Robert Morrison, sent out by the London Missionary Society in 1807, was the first Protestant missionary to reach the closed empire of China, entering under the shadow of a decree that made teaching the language to a foreigner a capital offence. He laboured a full seven years before he saw his first convert baptized, and in that patient obscurity he wrought the great work by which he is remembered: the translation of the whole Scriptures into Chinese, that a fifth of mankind might read the oracles of God in their own tongue. He compiled a Chinese dictionary that opened the door for every missionary who came after him, and he did it as a servant of the East India Company by day and a labourer for Christ by night, with little encouragement and much reproach. His life preaches that the Great Commission is fulfilled not chiefly by numbers seen in a season but by faithfulness sustained across barren years, and that the LORD honours the man who sows in tears the incorruptible seed of His written Word. Morrison confessed, when asked whether he expected to make an impression upon idolatrous China, that he did not, but that he expected God would; and in that answer lies the whole doctrine of providence which governed his toil. He died in Canton, having translated the Bible, buried a wife, and trusted that the harvest belonged to the Lord of the harvest alone.
webster_summary: The first Protestant missionary to China and translator of the Chinese Bible.
webster_full: A Scottish-descended Englishman (1782–1834), sent by the London Missionary Society, first Protestant missionary to the Chinese empire.
Translator of the whole of Scripture into Chinese, laid on the ground floor of gospel labour in the East.
Compiler of a monumental Chinese-English dictionary that equipped generations of missionaries who followed.
A man of long patience, waiting seven years before the baptism of his first convert, Tsae A-ko.
A pattern of quiet, providence-trusting faithfulness under a hostile and closed government.
scriptures: Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful.
He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him.
So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.
Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
corruption_summary: A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the principle of patient, Word-centred labour under providence.
corruption_paragraphs: Morrison’s name is preserved here not because any party has warped his memory into a heresy, but because his example rebukes the impatience of an age that measures gospel work by immediate visible returns. He answered a decade of apparent barrenness with translation, dictionary-making, and prayer, trusting the LORD to give the increase in His own time.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover from Morrison’s life is the sufficiency and centrality of the written Word: he judged that the surest gift he could leave to China was the Scriptures in her own tongue, believing with Isaiah that God’s Word would not return void. His seven-year wait recovers the doctrine of providence for us—that the times and seasons of the harvest are in the Father’s hand, and the steward’s whole duty is to be found faithful.
roots_summary: The name joins Germanic fame to Scottish sonship, but his true root was the sowing of the incorruptible seed.
roots_lines: Robert — Germanic Hrodebert, “bright in fame,” though his fame was hidden in Christ.
Morrison — “son of Morris,” a plain Northumberland lineage.
The deeper root: the incorruptible seed of the Word (1Pe 1:23), sown in a closed land.
A steward’s root in 1Co 4:2, required above all to be found faithful.
Grafted, like all the elect, into the true Vine from which alone his labour bore fruit.
usage: Cited as the father of Protestant missions to China, the first to render the whole Bible into Chinese.
Invoked as a pattern of patient, long-suffering faithfulness where visible fruit is long delayed.
Held up in missions history as proof that translation of the Word is enduring gospel labour.

etymology: Scottish; Alexander from the Greek Alexandros, “defender of men,” and Duff, a Highland surname from the Gaelic dubh, “dark.” Borne by the pioneering missionary-educator of India (1806–1878).
biblical_def: Alexander Duff, the first missionary sent abroad by the Church of Scotland, reached Calcutta in 1830 after twice suffering shipwreck on the passage, his library lost to the sea both times save for a Bible that floated to shore. Persuaded that the strongholds of Hindu learning must be met on the ground of learning itself, he established schools in which the whole compass of Western knowledge was taught, yet always as the handmaid of the truth, that the light of the gospel might break in upon the darkened understanding of the highest castes. He set the English tongue and the sciences at the service of Christ, reasoning that a false religion propped upon a false view of the world would fall when the true view of God’s creation was set before it, crowned always by the Scriptures. Many of the earliest and most notable converts of Bengal came through his lecture-hall, and his method shaped Protestant educational missions across India for a century. His life preaches that the gospel does not fear the schoolroom but sanctifies it, that every faculty of man is to be brought captive to the obedience of Christ, and that the LORD raises up learned men to storm the citadels of learned error. Returning broken in health to Scotland, Duff pleaded the cause of missions until his death, a defender of men indeed, but chiefly a servant of the God who defends His own.
webster_summary: The pioneer of Christian higher education as a missionary method in India.
webster_full: A Scot (1806–1878), first foreign missionary of the Church of Scotland, sent to Bengal in 1830.
Founder of a system of Christian schools teaching Western learning as the servant of the gospel.
Survivor of two shipwrecks on his outward voyages, his floated Bible a token of providence.
An advocate whose plea for missions stirred the churches of Scotland and beyond.
A pioneer whose educational method shaped Protestant missions across India for generations.
scriptures: Casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ;
Pro 4:7
Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding.
Dan 12:3
And they that be wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament; and they that turn many to righteousness as the stars for ever and ever.
The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.
corruption_summary: A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the principle that all true learning is subject to Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Duff’s memory is preserved not as a disputed teaching but as a standing witness that the gospel need not retreat before the learning of the world. He met the pride of Hindu scholarship not by shunning knowledge but by consecrating it, that the light of Scripture might expose the darkness of idolatry.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover from Duff’s labour is that wisdom is the principal thing and that every high thing which exalts itself against the knowledge of God must be cast down and brought captive to the obedience of Christ. His schools stand against the notion that faith and understanding are enemies, and remind the church that the God who made the mind commands its worship.
roots_summary: A defender-of-men by name who found his root in the wisdom that begins with the fear of the LORD.
roots_lines: Alexander — Greek Alexandros, “defender of men,” borne fitly by a contender for truth.
Duff — Gaelic dubh, “dark,” yet he carried light into darkness.
The root of wisdom: the fear of the LORD (Pro 9:10), which he set above all learning.
Grounded in 2Co 10:5, bringing every thought captive to Christ.
A star turning many to righteousness, promised to shine for ever (Dan 12:3).
usage: Named as the pioneer of educational missions, teaching Western science under the lordship of Christ.
Cited for the principle that learning must be sanctified, not feared, in the service of the gospel.
Remembered for the shipwrecks in which his Bible alone was preserved to him.

etymology: Welsh and biblical; Timothy from the Greek Timotheos, “honouring God,” the name of Paul’s beloved son in the faith, and Richard from the Germanic Ricohard, “strong ruler.” Borne by the Welsh Baptist missionary to China (1845–1919).
biblical_def: Timothy Richard, a Welsh Baptist sent to China in 1870, laboured through decades of that land’s upheaval, and is chiefly honoured for his tireless relief of the poor and suffering, most notably in the great northern famine of the late 1870s, when he spent himself in feeding the starving and pressing the gospel upon a broken people. He believed the church must reach the whole man, and threw himself into the education, reform, and evangelizing of a vast heathen nation. His compassion in famine, his readiness to labour where death and misery reigned, and his zeal to make Christ known set a mark upon Protestant missions in China. Yet in his later years his esteem for the ancient religions of the East softened into a broad hope that the world’s faiths might somehow converge, a drift the church must name plainly as departure from the exclusive gospel of Christ, who alone is the way, the truth, and the life. The good in Richard—his mercy to the perishing, his industry, his love of a people not his own—we honour heartily; the erring in him—the blunting of the offence of the cross and the notion that other religions carry saving light—we must reject as error, for there is none other name under heaven whereby men must be saved. His life is thus both a summons to mercy and a warning that compassion untethered from the exclusivity of Christ loses the very gospel it means to give.
webster_summary: A Welsh Baptist missionary to China, mighty in famine relief, later erring toward religious inclusivism.
webster_full: A Welshman (1845–1919), Baptist Missionary Society worker in China from 1870.
A labourer of great compassion, spending himself in the northern famine relief of the late 1870s.
A promoter of education and reform among the Chinese as avenues for the gospel.
A man whose later years drifted toward a hope of convergence among the world religions—an error the church must name.
A mixed example: mercy to the perishing to be honoured, doctrinal drift to be rejected.
scriptures: Act 4:12
Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved.
Joh 14:6
Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.
For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me in:
Gal 1:8
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
corruption_summary: A genuine mixture: his famine mercy is honourable, but his later religious inclusivism is real error the church must name.
corruption_paragraphs: Unlike most figures in this dictionary, Richard presents a genuine mixture to be weighed. His labours in famine and his love for the Chinese poor are truly honourable, an image of Christ feeding the hungry and taking in the stranger. These we praise without reserve, as the fruit of a compassionate spirit spent for a perishing people.

But his later softening toward the ancient religions of China, and his hope that the world’s faiths might converge upon a common light, must be named plainly as error and not as breadth of vision. Scripture forecloses the notion: there is salvation in no other name, and Christ alone is the way to the Father. A gospel that dulls the offence of the cross to accommodate false religion is another gospel, and Paul pronounces it accursed. Richard’s drift is a warning that mercy must never be allowed to melt down the exclusivity of Christ.
roots_summary: Named to honour God, yet his later error dishonoured the one name in which alone is salvation.
roots_lines: Timothy — Greek Timotheos, “honouring God,” Paul’s own son in the faith.
Richard — Germanic Ricohard, “strong ruler.”
The root that must hold: the exclusive name of Act 4:12, given for salvation.
Christ the sole way, truth, and life of Joh 14:6—a root his later thought loosened.
The warning of Gal 1:8 against any other gospel, however compassionately dressed.
usage: Cited for heroic famine relief and compassion toward the suffering poor of China.
Named also as a cautionary case where esteem for false religion eroded the exclusive gospel.
Studied where the church weighs the boundary between mercy ministry and doctrinal fidelity.

etymology: Welsh; Griffith from the Welsh Gruffudd, perhaps “strong lord” or “strong in faith,” and John from the Hebrew Yochanan, “the LORD is gracious.” Borne by the Welsh missionary to central China (1831–1912).
biblical_def: Griffith John, a Welshman set apart to preach almost from boyhood, was sent by the London Missionary Society to China in 1855, and for well-nigh sixty years laboured in the heart of that land, chiefly at Hankow on the Yangtze, planting the gospel where no missionary had gone before. He was above all a preacher and an itinerant, journeying through the interior provinces with the word of the cross upon his lips, and he poured his strength into rendering the Scriptures and gospel tracts into the tongues of the people, that the seed might be scattered widely by the printed page. Declining honours and calls that would have removed him from the field, he chose to spend and be spent in central China, esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the applause of men. His life preaches the primacy of preaching in the Great Commission—that it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe—and the perseverance of a servant who counts not his life dear unto himself so that he might finish his course with joy. Broken at last in body and sight, he returned to Britain only to die, having given the whole of his manhood to a people who had no claim upon him but the claim of Christ crucified. The LORD is gracious, his name declares; and that grace was the whole spring of a labour that spanned two generations without turning back.
webster_summary: A Welsh missionary who preached and translated in central China for nearly sixty years.
webster_full: A Welshman (1831–1912), sent by the London Missionary Society to China in 1855.
A pioneer of the interior, planting the gospel chiefly at Hankow on the Yangtze River.
An indefatigable preacher and itinerant, carrying the word of the cross into unreached provinces.
A translator who laboured to put Scripture and tracts into the tongues of the Chinese people.
A man who declined honours and calls home to spend near sixty years upon one field.
scriptures: For after that in the wisdom of God the world by wisdom knew not God, it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe.

But none of these things move me, neither count I my life dear unto myself, so that I might finish my course with joy, and the ministry, which I have received of the Lord Jesus, to testify the gospel of the grace of God.
How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher?
I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith:
corruption_summary: A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the primacy of preaching in the Great Commission.
corruption_paragraphs: Griffith John’s name is preserved not because any error has fastened upon it, but because his half-century of itinerant preaching rebukes an age uncertain whether the plain proclamation of the cross is still the ordained means of salvation. He staked his whole life on the answer that it is.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover from his labour is the primacy of preaching: it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe, and men cannot believe in Him of whom they have not heard. His sixty years also recover the doctrine of perseverance, for like Paul he counted not his life dear unto himself, that he might finish his course with joy.
roots_summary: His surname confesses that the LORD is gracious, and that grace was the root of a lifelong labour.
roots_lines: Griffith — Welsh Gruffudd, “strong lord” or “strong in faith.”
John — Hebrew Yochanan, “the LORD is gracious,” the wellspring of his ministry.
Rooted in Rom 10:14—none can hear without a preacher, and he was that preacher.
Grounded in Act 20:24, counting his life not dear so as to finish his course.
A root in the foolishness of preaching (1Co 1:21) by which God is pleased to save.
usage: Cited as a pioneer preacher of the Chinese interior, chiefly at Hankow on the Yangtze.
Named for a near-sixty-year ministry of itinerant preaching and Scripture translation.
Held up as an example of persevering, self-forgetful labour that declined ease and honour.

etymology: Scottish; William from the Germanic Willahelm, “resolute helmet” or “protector,” and Milne, a northern Scots surname denoting one who dwelt or worked at a mill. Borne by Morrison’s colleague in the China mission (1785–1822).
biblical_def: William Milne, an Aberdeenshire shepherd boy of poor estate and little schooling, was raised up by the LORD and sent by the London Missionary Society in 1813 to join Robert Morrison in the perilous work among the Chinese. Forbidden a settled place in Canton, he removed to Malacca, and there he founded the Anglo-Chinese College and a printing press, opening a base from which the gospel and the Scriptures might be carried to the scattered Chinese of the East Indies and beyond. He laboured with Morrison upon the translation of the Bible into Chinese, taking to himself a large share of the Old Testament, and he poured out his brief strength in preaching, printing, and training, that others might follow after him into the harvest. When Milne first sought a place with the mission, one committee thought his gifts too small; but the LORD delights to use the mean things of the world, and this untaught herdsman became a chief pillar of the China mission and a translator of holy Scripture. Cut down by consumption at only thirty-six, his years were few but his labours weighty, a rebuke to every man who despises the day of small things or who esteems himself too lowly to be useful to Christ. His life preaches that God chooses the base and the despised to confound the mighty, and that a short course faithfully run is honoured of Him who numbers the days of His servants.
webster_summary: Morrison’s colleague in China, founder of the Anglo-Chinese College at Malacca and Bible translator.
webster_full: A Scot (1785–1822), an untaught Aberdeenshire shepherd boy raised up for the China mission.
Sent by the London Missionary Society in 1813 to labour beside Robert Morrison.
Founder at Malacca of the Anglo-Chinese College and a printing press for gospel work.
A translator of Scripture into Chinese, bearing a large share of the Old Testament.
A man of few years, dead of consumption at thirty-six, yet weighty in lasting labour.
scriptures: But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty;
Zec 4:10

For who hath despised the day of small things? for they shall rejoice, and shall see the plummet in the hand of Zerubbabel with those seven; they are the eyes of the LORD, which run to and fro through the whole earth.
So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.
Mat 9:38
Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he will send forth labourers into his harvest.
corruption_summary: A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers that God chooses the base to confound the mighty.
corruption_paragraphs: Milne’s name is preserved not because error has touched it, but because his rise from an untaught shepherd boy to a translator of Scripture answers the pride of an age that measures usefulness by credentials rather than by the calling of God. One committee thought him too small; the LORD thought otherwise.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover from Milne’s life is that God hath chosen the weak and the foolish things of the world to confound the mighty, and that none should despise the day of small things. His death at thirty-six teaches us to number our days and apply our hearts unto wisdom, since the measure of a life is not its length but its faithfulness to the Lord of the harvest.
roots_summary: A miller’s and protector’s name, but his root was the God who exalts the lowly for His service.
roots_lines: William — Germanic Willahelm, “resolute helmet,” a protector’s name.
Milne — a Scots surname for one who dwelt or laboured at the mill.
Rooted in 1Co 1:27—God choosing the weak to confound the mighty.
Grounded in Zec 4:10, refusing to despise the day of small things.
A labourer sent by prayer into the harvest (Mat 9:38) though counted too small by men.
usage: Cited as Morrison’s chief colleague and co-translator in the early China mission.
Named as founder of the Anglo-Chinese College and press at Malacca.
Held up as proof that God exalts the lowly and honours a short life faithfully spent.

etymology: German; Karl from the Germanic karl, “free man” or “husbandman,” and Gützlaff, a Pomeranian surname. Borne by the German pioneer missionary along the China coast (1803–1851).
biblical_def: Karl Gützlaff, a Pomeranian sent first to the East Indies and then drawn to China, became one of the earliest and most daring evangelists along the coast of that closed empire, voyaging in Chinese dress aboard trading and coasting vessels to scatter Scriptures and tracts in ports where no missionary was permitted to dwell. He mastered the languages and dialects with rare quickness, laboured at Bible translation, served as interpreter, and set his heart on the whole of China at a time when the church scarcely dared to think of it. His burning vision, that the millions of the interior might be reached, kindled zeal in others and stirred the founding of societies to send labourers into that vast field, so that men such as Hudson Taylor drew fire from his example. Yet his boldness outran his prudence: the native colporteurs he trusted too readily sometimes deceived him, taking his money while burying rather than distributing his tracts, and his methods drew just criticism for want of care. We honour his holy ambition and his fearless love for a perishing people, while owning that zeal must be governed by wisdom, lest the good seed be entrusted to unfaithful hands. His life preaches both the largeness of vision the Great Commission demands and the sober watchfulness it requires, that a man be not only bold for Christ but faithful and discerning in the stewardship committed to him.
webster_summary: A German pioneer evangelist along the China coast whose vast vision stirred later missions.
webster_full: A Pomeranian German (1803–1851), an early and daring evangelist along the coast of China.
A voyager in Chinese dress, scattering Scriptures and tracts in ports closed to missionaries.
A rapid master of languages, translator, and interpreter in the service of the gospel.
A kindler of missionary zeal whose vision for all China inspired Hudson Taylor and others.
A bold labourer whose want of prudence in trusting native agents drew just criticism.
scriptures: And how shall they preach, except they be sent? as it is written, How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace, and bring glad tidings of good things!
Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful.
Pro 19:2
Also, that the soul be without knowledge, it is not good; and he that hasteth with his feet sinneth.
Mat 9:37
Then saith he unto his disciples, The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few;
corruption_summary: A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers bold vision tempered by faithful stewardship.
corruption_paragraphs: Gützlaff’s name is preserved not as a disputed teaching but as an example both to imitate and to sober us. His holy ambition for the whole of China rebukes small faith, while the abuse of his trust by unfaithful colporteurs rebukes zeal that outruns discernment.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover from his life is that bold gospel vision must be joined to faithful stewardship: it is beautiful that men be sent to preach, yet it is required in stewards that they be found faithful, and Proverbs warns that he who hastens with his feet sinneth. Gützlaff teaches the church to be at once large-hearted for the harvest and watchful over the means, that the good seed be not squandered by careless hands.
roots_summary: A free man by name, his root was a heart enlarged for the harvest, though needing wisdom’s bridle.
roots_lines: Karl — Germanic karl, “free man” or “husbandman” of the harvest.
Gützlaff — a Pomeranian surname of the German coastlands.
Rooted in Rom 10:15—beautiful feet of them that are sent to preach.
Bridled by 1Co 4:2, requiring stewards to be found faithful, not merely bold.
Warned by Pro 19:2 that haste without knowledge is not good.
usage: Cited as a pioneer coastal evangelist who scattered Scripture where missionaries could not dwell.
Named as an inspirer of Hudson Taylor and the founding of interior-China missions.
Studied for the lesson that missionary boldness must be governed by prudence and faithful oversight.

etymology: Scottish; Alexander from the Greek Alexandros, “defender of men,” and Mackay from the Gaelic Mac Aoidh, “son of Aodh” (a fire-god name meaning “fire”). Borne by the engineer-missionary to Uganda (1849–1890).
biblical_def: Alexander Mackay, a Scottish engineer moved by Stanley’s call for labourers, sailed in 1876 with the Church Missionary Society to Uganda, and there gave the whole of his manhood to the peoples about Lake Victoria until fever took him at forty-one, having never once come home. He wrought as an engineer for Christ, cutting roads, building boats, setting up a printing press, and teaching useful arts, believing that the gospel dignifies labour and that the Word must go forth in the mother tongue. He translated portions of Scripture into the Ganda language, that a newly reached people might read of their Saviour, and he stood immovable through years of peril, court intrigue, and the fires of persecution. It was in his day that the young Ugandan converts, refusing to renounce Christ, were burned alive by the king’s command—the noble army of the Uganda martyrs—and their steadfastness, watered by Mackay’s teaching, remains a witness that the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the church. When others fled, he chose to remain, that the little flock might not be left shepherdless. His life preaches that skilled hands and a sanctified trade may serve the Great Commission as truly as the pulpit, and that faithful endurance unto death, whether the missionary’s or the convert’s, is precious in the sight of the LORD, whose saints are honoured though the world counts their deaths a waste.
webster_summary: A Scottish engineer-missionary who gave his life to Uganda and taught its noble army of martyrs.
webster_full: A Scot (1849–1890), an engineer sent by the Church Missionary Society to Uganda in 1876.
A builder of roads, boats, and a printing press, dignifying labour in the service of the gospel.
A translator of Scripture portions into the Ganda tongue for a newly reached people.
A steadfast witness through the persecution that martyred the young Ugandan converts.
A man who never returned home, dying of fever at forty-one on the field he loved.
scriptures: Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints.
Rev 2:10

Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer: behold, the devil shall cast some of you into prison, that ye may be tried; and ye shall have tribulation ten days: be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.
Col 3:23
And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men;

corruption_summary: A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers that consecrated labour and endurance unto death serve the gospel.
corruption_paragraphs: Mackay’s name is preserved not because any error clings to it, but because his engineer’s consecration and his fellowship with martyrs answer an age that severs faith from work and shrinks from suffering. He built and translated and stayed while others fled.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover from his life is twofold: first, that whatsoever we do is to be done heartily as to the Lord, so that a sanctified trade serves Christ as truly as the pulpit; and second, that faithfulness unto death is crowned by the Lord, for precious in His sight is the death of His saints. The Uganda martyrs he taught proclaim that the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the church.
roots_summary: Named “son of fire,” his root was a fire of love that burned to death on the field for Christ.
roots_lines: Alexander — Greek Alexandros, “defender of men.”
Mackay — Gaelic Mac Aoidh, “son of fire,” aptly borne by a fervent labourer.
Rooted in Col 3:23—working heartily as to the Lord in every honest trade.
Grounded in Rev 2:10, faithful unto death for the crown of life.
A saint whose death was precious to the LORD (Psa 116:15) though far from home.
usage: Cited as the engineer-missionary who joined useful arts to gospel labour in Uganda.
Named in connection with the Uganda martyrs, whose steadfastness his teaching nourished.
Held up as a pattern of endurance, remaining at his post through persecution unto death.

etymology: French; François, “Frenchman” or “free one,” and Coillard, a French surname. Borne by the Huguenot-descended Protestant missionary to the Barotse of the upper Zambezi (1834–1904).
biblical_def: François Coillard, a Frenchman of Huguenot stock sent by the Paris Evangelical Missionary Society, gave his life first to the Basuto of southern Africa and then, in his later years, to the pioneering of a mission among the Barotse in the valley of the upper Zambezi, a region hard of access and long unreached by the gospel. With his devoted wife Christina at his side, he pressed into that far country, enduring the caprice of native kings, the ravages of fever, and the crushing loss of fellow labourers and of his beloved wife herself, yet he would not turn back from the door the LORD had opened. He translated and taught, planted the seed of the Word among a heathen people, and laid the foundations of a church in Barotseland at great and personal cost. His whole course was governed by a settled trust in the providence of God, and when hindered on every side he was wont to say that when God shuts one door He opens another. His life preaches that the pioneer’s path is a way of sacrifice and bereavement, that the gospel advances often through the graves of those who carry it, and that the servant who walks by faith may commit both his losses and his labours to a Father who does all things well. The blood and tears of the Coillards became, under God, the seed of a church among a people once wholly in darkness.
webster_summary: A Huguenot-descended missionary who pioneered the gospel among the Barotse of the Zambezi.
webster_full: A Frenchman (1834–1904) of Huguenot descent, sent by the Paris Evangelical Missionary Society.
A labourer first among the Basuto, then a pioneer to the Barotse of the upper Zambezi.
A husband whose wife Christina shared his toils and whose loss he bore in the field.
A translator and teacher who planted a church in Barotseland at great personal cost.
A man of settled trust in providence, holding that when God shuts one door He opens another.

Rom 8:28
And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose.

These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.
corruption_summary: A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers providence and sacrifice in pioneer missions.
corruption_paragraphs: Coillard’s name is preserved not because error has fastened upon it, but because his sacrifice and his unshaken confidence in providence rebuke an age that expects gospel advance without cost or bereavement. He buried his wife and fellow labourers, yet held to the open door.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover from his life is that the pioneer’s path is one of sacrifice, and that except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die it abideth alone. His trust that all things work together for good to them that love God, and his confidence in the door no man can shut, recover for us the doctrine of providence, under which the servant may commit his griefs and his gains alike to a Father who does all things well.
roots_summary: A Huguenot root nourished his faith; the deeper root was the wheat-corn dying to bring forth much fruit.
roots_lines: François — “Frenchman” or “free one,” of Huguenot lineage.
Coillard — a French surname carried into the African interior.
Rooted in Joh 12:24—the corn of wheat dying to bring forth much fruit.
Grounded in Rom 8:28, all things working together for good to them that love God.
A pilgrim who died in faith, seeing the promises afar off (Heb 11:13).
usage: Cited as the pioneer missionary to the Barotse of the upper Zambezi.
Named for his settled trust in providence amid bereavement and hardship.
Held up as an example that gospel advance often comes through sacrifice and loss.

etymology: Scottish; Robert from the Germanic Hrodebert, “bright in fame,” and Laws, a Scots surname denoting one who dwelt by a low rounded hill (a “law”). Borne by the missionary of Livingstonia on Lake Nyasa (1851–1934).
biblical_def: Robert Laws, a Scot trained in both medicine and divinity, went out in 1875 to the shores of Lake Nyasa in the mission named Livingstonia in honour of David Livingstone, and there he laboured for more than half a century in what is now Malawi, giving his whole life to a people sunk in heathenism and long ravaged by the cruelties of the slave trade. He was physician, preacher, translator, and teacher, joining the healing of bodies to the saving of souls, and he built at Livingstonia an institution that trained African men in the Scriptures, in useful arts, and in godliness, so that the gospel might take root and be carried forward by the sons of the land themselves. He believed that the surest fruit of missions is a native church, self-supporting and self-propagating, and he spent his strength to that end, that the light he had brought might not depart with him but abide among a people made his own in Christ. Fifty-two years he stayed, watching the wilderness become a garden of the LORD where slave-raiders had once made a desolation. His life preaches the wholeness of gospel mercy, that Christ’s servants tend both the body and the soul, and that the true aim of missions is not a dependent flock but a rooted church, planted, watered, and given the increase by God, that shall stand and bear fruit long after the labourer is gathered to his rest.
webster_summary: A Scottish physician-missionary who gave fifty-two years to Livingstonia on Lake Nyasa.
webster_full: A Scot (1851–1934), trained in medicine and divinity, sent to Lake Nyasa in 1875.
A founder and leader of the Livingstonia mission in what is now Malawi.
A physician, preacher, and translator who joined healing of the body to saving of the soul.
A builder of an institution training Africans in Scripture, godliness, and useful arts.
A labourer of fifty-two years who aimed at a self-supporting, self-propagating native church.
scriptures: I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase.
Mat 4:23
And Jesus went about all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, and preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing all manner of sickness and all manner of disease among the people.
Isa 35:1
The wilderness and the solitary place shall be glad for them; and the desert shall rejoice, and blossom as the rose.
They shall still bring forth fruit in old age; they shall be fat and flourishing;
corruption_summary: A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers whole-souled mercy and the planting of a rooted native church.
corruption_paragraphs: Laws’s name is preserved not because error has touched it, but because his half-century of medicine, teaching, and church-planting answers an age uncertain whether missions should heal the body, whether they should aim at a self-sustaining church, and whether one man’s lifelong perseverance can turn a desert into a garden. His answer was yes on every count.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover from his life is that gospel mercy is whole, tending body and soul as Christ Himself did, and that the true end of missions is a rooted native church: one plants, another waters, but God gives the increase. His fifty-two years, bringing forth fruit even in old age, testify that the wilderness shall blossom as the rose where the LORD is at work.
roots_summary: Bright in fame by name, his root was the planting that God alone makes to grow.
roots_lines: Robert — Germanic Hrodebert, “bright in fame.”
Laws — a Scots surname for one dwelling by a low rounded hill.
Rooted in 1Co 3:6—he planted, but God gave the increase.
Grounded in Mat 4:23, joining healing of the body to preaching of the kingdom.
A tree still bringing forth fruit in old age (Psa 92:14) beside Lake Nyasa.
usage: Cited as the physician-missionary and long-serving leader of Livingstonia on Lake Nyasa.
Named for joining medical mercy to gospel preaching among a slave-ravaged people.
Held up for the aim of a self-supporting, self-propagating native church.

etymology: English and biblical; Lott, a form of the Hebrew Lot, “covering” or “veil,” and Carey, an English surname. Borne by the freed slave and Baptist missionary to Liberia (c. 1780–1828).
biblical_def: Lott Carey, born a slave in Virginia, was brought under the power of the gospel and, converting to Christ, laboured to purchase his own freedom and that of his children, being made free by the truth that had already made him free indeed. Not content to keep his liberty to himself, this once-enslaved man became a Baptist preacher and, in 1821, sailed for Africa as one of the first American missionaries to that continent, planting the gospel and a church in the new settlement of Liberia, and ministering as pastor, physician, and civic leader to a struggling colony of freed men. He counted the reproach of Africa greater riches than the ease he might have kept, declaring that he wished to go where he might be estimated by his character and not by his complexion, and above all where he might carry Christ to a people in darkness. His life preaches the sovereign grace that lifts a bondman to be an ambassador of the King of kings, the Great Commission laid upon every believer without respect of estate or birth, and the liberty of the gospel which, having freed the soul, sends it forth to free others by the same Word. He died in Liberia in the midst of his labours, a monument to the truth that the LORD makes His freedmen into His messengers, and that no man is too lowly born to be sent by God to the ends of the earth.
webster_summary: A freed Virginia slave who became one of the first American missionaries to Africa, in Liberia.
webster_full: A Virginian (c. 1780–1828), born a slave, converted to Christ, and purchaser of his own freedom.
A Baptist preacher who sailed for Africa in 1821 as an early American missionary.
A founder of gospel work and a church in the settlement of Liberia.
A pastor, physician, and leader to a struggling colony of freed men.
A monument to sovereign grace lifting a bondman into an ambassador of Christ.
scriptures: Joh 8:36
If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed.
Now then we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God did beseech you by us: we pray you in Christ’s stead, be ye reconciled to God.
Gal 3:28
There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus.
Act 8:4
Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word.
corruption_summary: A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers gospel liberty sending the freed soul to free others.
corruption_paragraphs: Carey’s name is preserved not because any party has warped it into a heresy, but because his rise from slavery to missionary declares that the Great Commission rests upon every believer without respect of estate, and that the grace which frees a soul makes it a herald of freedom to others.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover from Carey’s life is the liberty of the gospel: if the Son makes a man free, he is free indeed, and being freed he is made an ambassador for Christ, beseeching men to be reconciled to God. In Christ there is neither bond nor free, and this once-enslaved man, sent to Africa, proves that God calls whom He will, that the scattered may go everywhere preaching the word.
roots_summary: A veil by name, but the veil was taken away in Christ, who made the bondman free to serve.
roots_lines: Lott — a form of Hebrew Lot, “covering” or “veil.”
Carey — an English surname borne into missionary service.
Rooted in Joh 8:36—made free indeed by the Son of God.
Grounded in 2Co 5:20, an ambassador for Christ though once a slave.
One in Christ where there is neither bond nor free (Gal 3:28).
usage: Cited as a freed slave who became one of the first American missionaries to Africa.
Named as a founder of gospel work and a church in early Liberia.
Held up as proof that God sends messengers without respect of birth or estate.
